hook.text: White crust on farmland soil is a death sentence. That's salt—and once it's there, crops can't grow.

buildup.text: Irrigation water carries dissolved salts. When water evaporates, salt stays behind and accumulates over time.

discovery.text: About 20% of the world's irrigated farmland suffers from salt buildup. That's 62 million hectares damaged.

twist.text: Australia lost vast areas to salinization after clearing deep-rooted trees. The water table rose, bringing salt up.

climax.text: Fixing salinization requires flushing fields with excess water—expensive and itself water-wasting.

punchline.text: Irrigation gives water. Evaporation leaves the bill—in salt.

quiz.question: What percentage of the world's irrigated land is affected by salinization?

details.summary: Soil salinization is the accumulation of soluble salts in soil to levels toxic to crops. It affects an estimated 1 billion hectares globally and is worsening due to irrigation practices that raise salty groundwater or leave salt residues as water evaporates.
details.whyItMatters: Salinization has destroyed agricultural civilizations throughout history—from ancient Mesopotamia to modern Australia. Irrigation-induced salinization threatens 20% of the world's irrigated land, which produces one-third of global food.
takeaways: Salinization affects roughly 1 billion hectares of land globally and is growing
Irrigation is the primary cause—evaporation concentrates salts in the root zone
Most crops cannot tolerate electrical conductivity above 4 dS/m in soil water

faq.question: How does irrigation cause soil salinization?
faq.answer: Irrigation water always contains some dissolved salts. When water evaporates or is consumed by plants, salts remain in the soil and accumulate over time. Rising water tables from over-irrigation bring deeper salty groundwater to the root zone, further concentrating salts.

faq.question: Can salt-damaged soil be restored to productive farmland?
faq.answer: Leaching with excess water can flush salts below the root zone if drainage is adequate. Gypsum application helps displace sodium from clay particles. Salt-tolerant crops like barley and certain grasses can be grown during remediation.
